title: Conservation of Energy and Resources
unitGoal: Students will compare energy sources, understand resource use, and practise stewardship-minded choices that conserve energy and materials.

lessons.title: Forms of Energy in Everyday Life
lessons.learningGoal: Students will identify common forms of energy and describe how they are used in everyday devices and systems.
successCriteria: I can identify light, sound, thermal, electrical, mechanical, and chemical energy.
I can match forms of energy to everyday examples.
I can explain that useful devices often involve more than one form of energy.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise identifying common forms of energy in everyday examples.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that energy is needed for change and motion and that energy appears in several useful forms.
lessons.christianFocus: Students study energy as part of God's orderly created world and consider how energy should be used wisely.
lessonContent: Energy is the ability to cause change or do work.
Light energy lets us see and can be produced by the sun, lamps, and screens.
Sound energy is produced by vibrations.
Thermal energy is connected to temperature and heat transfer.
Electrical energy powers many devices and can be changed into other forms.
Mechanical energy is connected to movement and position.
Chemical energy is stored in substances such as food, batteries, and fuels.

studentActivity.title: Forms of Energy Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise spotting forms of energy in everyday examples.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: energy has different forms
steps.text: Energy is needed for motion, light, sound, heat, and many changes. Grade 5 students should be able to name common forms of energy and match them to examples.

steps.title: Six Common Forms
steps.prompt: Look for what is happening
steps.text: Light, sound, thermal, electrical, mechanical, and chemical energy are common forms. A device or living thing may involve more than one form at the same time.

steps.title: Light
steps.prompt: Which example mainly shows light energy being used?
choices: a lamp helping a student read
a backpack resting on the floor
a closed book sitting on a shelf
steps.correctAnswer: a lamp helping a student read
steps.feedback: Correct. The lamp gives off light energy.
steps.hint: Look for seeing or illumination.

steps.title: Sound
steps.prompt: Which example mainly shows sound energy?
choices: a bell vibrating after it is struck
a battery stored in a drawer
steps.correctAnswer: a bell vibrating after it is struck
steps.feedback: Yes. Sound comes from vibrations.
steps.hint: Sound needs vibrations.

steps.title: Chemical
steps.prompt: Which example includes stored chemical energy?
choices: food that the body can use
a pencil lying still on a desk
steps.correctAnswer: food that the body can use
steps.feedback: Correct. Food stores chemical energy.
steps.hint: Think about stored energy in substances.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Thermal energy is connected to temperature and heat transfer.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Thermal energy is linked to heat.
steps.hint: Warm and cool objects involve thermal energy.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised naming forms of energy.

steps.title: Devices Can Use Several Forms
steps.prompt: Follow the energy
steps.text: A device may take in one form of energy and give off another. A speaker uses electrical energy to produce sound. A toaster uses electrical energy to produce thermal energy.

steps.title: Speaker
steps.prompt: A small speaker plays music from a tablet. Which energy change is most important?
choices: mechanical energy to stored food energy
steps.correctAnswer: electrical energy to sound energy
steps.feedback: Correct. The speaker uses electrical energy to make sound.
steps.hint: The output is music you hear.

steps.title: Toaster
steps.prompt: A toaster warms bread. Which energy form is the useful output?
steps.correctAnswer: thermal energy
steps.feedback: Yes. The toaster's useful output is heat.
steps.hint: The bread gets warmer.

steps.title: Moving Fan
steps.prompt: An electric fan spins its blades. Which energy form is shown by the moving blades?
steps.correctAnswer: mechanical energy
steps.feedback: Correct. Moving parts show mechanical energy.
steps.hint: Movement is the clue.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A device can involve more than one form of energy.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Many devices transform energy.
steps.hint: Think about a lamp that gives light and also warms up.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised identifying energy in devices.

questions.correctAnswer: Energy is the ability to cause change or do work.
questions.reviewNote: Energy is needed for work and change.

choices: a flashlight shining on a path

questions.correctAnswer: a mug of hot soup cooling on a table
questions.reviewNote: Thermal energy is linked to heat.

questions.correctAnswer: a battery

questions.correctAnswer: True

lessons.title: Renewable and Non-Renewable Energy Sources
lessons.learningGoal: Students will compare renewable and non-renewable energy sources using benefits, limits, reliability, and stewardship concerns.
successCriteria: I can identify renewable and non-renewable energy sources.
I can compare benefits and limits of different energy sources.
I can explain why energy choices often involve trade-offs.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise comparing energy sources without oversimplifying their benefits and limits.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that energy sources can be renewable or non-renewable and that wise decisions compare reliability, cost, impact, and use.
lessons.christianFocus: Students practise stewardship by thinking carefully about how people use the resources God has provided.
lessonContent: An energy source is something people use to get useful energy.
Renewable energy sources can be replenished naturally in a relatively short time, such as sunlight, wind, moving water, and plant material.
Non-renewable energy sources are used much faster than they are replaced, such as coal, oil, natural gas, and uranium.
Every energy source has benefits and limits.
Good decisions compare reliability, cost, location, technology, environmental effects, and human needs.

studentActivity.title: Energy Sources Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise comparing renewable and non-renewable energy sources.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: energy comes from sources
steps.text: People use different energy sources for heat, electricity, transportation, and machines. Some sources are renewable, and some are non-renewable.

steps.title: Renewable and Non-Renewable
steps.prompt: Think about replacement time
steps.text: Renewable sources are replenished naturally in a short time. Non-renewable sources are used much faster than they are replaced. Both kinds should be studied honestly.

steps.title: Renewable Example
steps.prompt: Which energy source is renewable?
steps.correctAnswer: wind
steps.feedback: Correct. Wind is naturally replenished.
steps.hint: Think about what can be replaced in a short time.

steps.title: Non-Renewable Example
steps.prompt: Which energy source is non-renewable?
steps.correctAnswer: oil
steps.feedback: Yes. Oil is used much faster than it is replaced.
steps.hint: Think about underground fuels.

steps.title: Uranium
steps.prompt: Why is uranium usually classified as non-renewable?
choices: It is a limited resource mined from the earth.
It is produced daily by wind turbines.
It is the same as sunlight in every way.
steps.correctAnswer: It is a limited resource mined from the earth.
steps.feedback: Correct. Uranium is limited and mined.
steps.hint: Non-renewable does not only mean fuel that burns.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Renewable means the source is naturally replenished in a relatively short time.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Replacement time matters.
steps.hint: Renewable sources can be renewed naturally.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised sorting energy sources.

steps.title: No Source Is Perfect
steps.prompt: Compare benefits and limits
steps.text: Energy choices involve trade-offs. A source might be renewable but depend on weather. Another source might be reliable but create pollution or use a limited resource.

steps.title: Wind Trade-Off
steps.prompt: Which comparison is most accurate for wind energy?
choices: It is renewable, but its output can change with wind conditions.
It is non-renewable because turbines have moving parts.
It works exactly the same in every location.
steps.correctAnswer: It is renewable, but its output can change with wind conditions.
steps.feedback: Correct. Wind is renewable but variable.
steps.hint: Think about both benefit and limit.

steps.title: Fuel Trade-Off
steps.prompt: Which statement is most accurate about coal, oil, and natural gas?
choices: They can provide useful energy, but they are limited and can affect air quality.
They are renewable because people use them often.
They have no environmental effects when burned.
steps.correctAnswer: They can provide useful energy, but they are limited and can affect air quality.
steps.feedback: Yes. This answer names both usefulness and concern.
steps.hint: A fair comparison includes benefits and costs.

steps.title: Location
steps.prompt: Why does location matter when choosing an energy source?
choices: Some places have more wind, sunlight, moving water, or fuel access than others.
Location changes renewable sources into non-renewable sources.
All energy sources work equally well everywhere.
steps.correctAnswer: Some places have more wind, sunlight, moving water, or fuel access than others.
steps.feedback: Correct. Local conditions matter.
steps.hint: Energy decisions depend on place.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A wise energy decision should compare benefits, limits, and human needs.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Energy decisions involve trade-offs.
steps.hint: Simple one-word answers are usually not enough.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised comparing energy-source trade-offs.

questions.correctAnswer: sunlight
oil
questions.reviewNote: Oil is used faster than it is replaced.

choices: It is a limited mined resource.
It is created whenever sunlight shines.
questions.correctAnswer: It is a limited mined resource.

questions.prompt: Which statement about wind energy is most accurate?
choices: It is renewable, but output depends on wind conditions.
It is non-renewable because turbines are built from materials.
It has the same output in every location.
questions.correctAnswer: It is renewable, but output depends on wind conditions.
questions.reviewNote: Wind energy is renewable but variable.

questions.prompt: Which statement about coal, oil, and natural gas is most accurate?
choices: They provide useful energy but are limited and can affect air quality.
They are renewable because they are used often.
They have no effects when burned.
questions.correctAnswer: They provide useful energy but are limited and can affect air quality.

questions.prompt: Why does location matter for energy choices?
choices: Energy sources and conditions differ from place to place.
questions.correctAnswer: Energy sources and conditions differ from place to place.

questions.prompt: Renewable energy sources are replenished naturally in a relatively short time.
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: A fair comparison should include both benefits and limits.
questions.correctAnswer: True

lessons.title: Electricity, Heat, and Energy Choices
lessons.learningGoal: Students will explain energy transformations in electrical devices and describe how heat can be conserved or wasted.
successCriteria: I can identify energy transformations in common devices.
I can explain that some transformed energy may spread into the environment as heat, light, or sound.
I can choose technology or habits that reduce wasted energy.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise tracking energy transformations and choosing efficient habits and technologies.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that energy changes form in devices and that thoughtful design can reduce wasted energy.
lessons.christianFocus: Students practise stewardship by noticing ways to use energy wisely rather than carelessly.
lessonContent: Energy can be transformed from one form to another.
Electrical devices often transform electrical energy into light, sound, thermal energy, or motion.
Energy is not created or destroyed by a device; it changes form and may spread into the environment.
Some energy transformations are useful, while some energy spreads away as heat, light, or sound that was not the main purpose.
Insulation, efficient devices, and wise habits can reduce unnecessary energy loss.

studentActivity.title: Energy Transformation Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise following energy transformations and choosing efficient energy habits.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: energy changes form
steps.text: Energy can change from one form to another. A device usually takes in one form of energy and produces one or more outputs.

steps.title: Useful and Unwanted Outputs
steps.prompt: Not every output is the goal
steps.text: A lamp is meant to give light, but it may also get warm. A blender is meant to move blades, but it also makes sound. Some energy spreads away instead of doing the main job.

steps.title: Lamp
steps.prompt: In a lamp, what is the main useful energy output?
steps.correctAnswer: light energy
steps.feedback: Correct. A lamp's main job is to give light.
steps.hint: Think about why people turn on a lamp.

steps.title: Blender
steps.prompt: A blender changes electrical energy mainly into what useful form?
choices: chemical energy stored in the cord
steps.correctAnswer: mechanical energy of moving blades
steps.feedback: Yes. The blades move.
steps.hint: Look at the device's main job.

steps.title: Waste Heat
steps.prompt: A phone charger feels warm after use. What does this show?
choices: Some energy spread into the environment as thermal energy.
The charger created new energy from nothing.
steps.correctAnswer: Some energy spread into the environment as thermal energy.
steps.feedback: Correct. Some transformed energy can spread as heat.
steps.hint: Warmth is linked to thermal energy.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Energy can be transformed from one form to another.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Energy transformations happen in many devices.
steps.hint: Think about electricity becoming light or motion.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised following energy transformations.

steps.title: Efficiency and Insulation
steps.prompt: Use energy wisely
steps.text: Efficiency means getting more useful output from the energy used. Insulation slows heat transfer, which can help keep warm things warm or cool things cool.

steps.title: Insulation
steps.prompt: Why does a travel mug help a hot drink stay warm longer?
choices: Insulation slows heat transfer to the surroundings.
The mug creates extra heat from the air.
The mug removes the drink's thermal energy.
steps.correctAnswer: Insulation slows heat transfer to the surroundings.
steps.feedback: Correct. Insulation slows heat movement.
steps.hint: Insulation does not create heat; it slows transfer.

steps.title: Efficient Bulb
steps.prompt: Why might an LED bulb be chosen instead of an older bulb?
choices: It can provide useful light while wasting less energy as heat.
It changes all electricity into sound.
It makes electricity renewable by itself.
steps.correctAnswer: It can provide useful light while wasting less energy as heat.
steps.feedback: Yes. Efficient technology can reduce wasted energy.
steps.hint: Think about useful light and unwanted heat.

steps.title: Habit Choice
steps.prompt: Which habit reduces unnecessary electricity use?
choices: turning off lights in an empty room
opening a fridge door to cool the kitchen
running two devices when one is enough
steps.correctAnswer: turning off lights in an empty room
steps.feedback: Correct. Turning off unused devices conserves energy.
steps.hint: Use energy when it is needed.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Energy-saving choices can include both better technology and wiser habits.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Devices and habits both matter.
steps.hint: Conservation is not only about one tool.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised reducing wasted energy.

quiz.title: Electricity, Heat, and Energy Choices Quiz

questions.prompt: A lamp mainly transforms electrical energy into...
questions.correctAnswer: light energy

questions.prompt: An electric fan mainly transforms electrical energy into...
questions.correctAnswer: mechanical energy

questions.prompt: A charger gets warm. Which idea fits best?
choices: Some energy has spread as thermal energy.
The charger created energy from nothing.
The cord became a renewable source.
questions.correctAnswer: Some energy has spread as thermal energy.

questions.prompt: How does insulation help a hot drink?
choices: It changes the drink into electricity.
questions.correctAnswer: It slows heat transfer.

questions.prompt: Why can an efficient bulb conserve energy?
choices: It gives useful light while wasting less energy as heat.
It uses no energy at all.
It turns every kind of energy into coal.
questions.correctAnswer: It gives useful light while wasting less energy as heat.
questions.reviewNote: Efficiency means more useful output for the energy used.

choices: turn off lights in an empty room
leave a screen on overnight when not needed
open the fridge often to cool the room
questions.correctAnswer: turn off lights in an empty room
questions.reviewNote: Turning off unused devices conserves energy.

questions.prompt: Energy can be transformed from one form to another.
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: Some energy may spread into the environment as heat, light, or sound that was not the device's main purpose.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.reviewNote: Some output is not useful for the main task.

lessons.title: Conservation at Home and School
lessons.learningGoal: Students will identify practical conservation choices while respecting privacy and different family situations.
successCriteria: I can explain what conservation means.
I can identify conservation choices for shared spaces such as classrooms.
I can make respectful suggestions without judging private family choices.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise conservation choices for school and community without requiring private home details.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that conservation means using energy and resources wisely and that suggestions should be respectful and realistic.
lessons.christianFocus: Students connect conservation with stewardship, gratitude, and loving neighbours through responsible use of shared resources.
lessonContent: Conservation means using energy and resources wisely and avoiding unnecessary waste.
Students can practise conservation in shared spaces such as classrooms, libraries, church buildings, and community spaces.
Helpful conservation ideas are specific, realistic, and respectful.
Students should not be required to share private details about family income, bills, appliances, or home routines.
Small repeated habits can matter when many people practise them over time.

studentActivity.title: Conservation Choices Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise choosing respectful ways to conserve energy and resources.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: conservation means wise use
steps.text: Conservation is not only about using less. It means using energy and resources wisely, avoiding waste, and thinking about how choices affect others.

steps.title: Shared Spaces
steps.prompt: Practise with school examples
steps.text: It is often best to practise conservation with shared spaces. Students can discuss classroom lights, paper use, water use, and device charging without sharing private home details.

steps.title: Classroom Lights
steps.prompt: Which choice best shows energy conservation in a classroom?
choices: turn off lights when the room will be empty
turn on every light before leaving
cover the windows so daylight is never used
steps.correctAnswer: turn off lights when the room will be empty
steps.feedback: Correct. Turning off unused lights avoids waste.
steps.hint: Think about using energy only when needed.

steps.title: Paper Use
steps.prompt: Which choice best conserves paper during a draft-writing activity?
choices: use both sides or revise digitally when appropriate
throw away every draft after one sentence
print several copies before checking for mistakes
steps.correctAnswer: use both sides or revise digitally when appropriate
steps.feedback: Yes. This reduces unnecessary paper use.
steps.hint: Think about avoiding waste while still learning well.

steps.title: Water Use
steps.prompt: Which habit conserves water?
choices: turn off the tap while it is not being used
let the tap run while finding supplies
use extra water so the sink looks clean
steps.correctAnswer: turn off the tap while it is not being used
steps.feedback: Correct. Turning off unused water avoids waste.
steps.hint: Use water when needed.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Conservation means using energy and resources wisely, not wasting them carelessly.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Conservation is wise use.
steps.hint: Think stewardship.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised spotting conservation choices.

steps.title: Respect and Privacy
steps.prompt: Suggestions should be kind
steps.text: Good conservation suggestions do not shame people or demand private information. They name a realistic action and explain why it may help.

steps.title: Respectful Wording
steps.prompt: Which suggestion is most respectful?
choices: Could we turn off unused lights to save energy?
Your family must be wasting energy if your bill is high.
Only people with new appliances can conserve energy.
steps.correctAnswer: Could we turn off unused lights to save energy?
steps.feedback: Correct. It is specific and respectful.
steps.hint: Avoid judging private situations.

steps.title: Privacy
steps.prompt: Which question should a class conservation activity avoid asking students to share?
choices: How much does your family pay for electricity?
What is one way a classroom could waste less paper?
Why might a closed door help keep heat in a room?
steps.correctAnswer: How much does your family pay for electricity?
steps.feedback: Yes. Family bills are private.
steps.hint: Choose the question that asks for private information.

steps.title: Realistic Plan
steps.prompt: Which classroom plan is most realistic?
choices: Assign a helper to check unused lights and devices at the end of the day.
Stop using every device even when the teacher needs one for learning.
Never use paper again for any subject.
steps.correctAnswer: Assign a helper to check unused lights and devices at the end of the day.
steps.feedback: Correct. It is practical and respectful.
steps.hint: A good plan can actually be followed.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A conservation idea should be respectful of different family situations.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Conservation should not become shaming.
steps.hint: Stewardship should be gracious.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised respectful conservation suggestions.

quiz.title: Conservation at Home and School Quiz

choices: using energy and resources wisely and avoiding waste
never using any resources at all
using more materials so a project looks larger
questions.correctAnswer: using energy and resources wisely and avoiding waste

choices: turn off lights in an empty room
questions.correctAnswer: turn off lights in an empty room

choices: throw away paper after one sentence
questions.correctAnswer: use both sides when appropriate
questions.reviewNote: Using both sides can reduce waste.

choices: turn off the tap while not using it
let the tap run while walking away
use extra water to make a sink sound busy
questions.correctAnswer: turn off the tap while not using it
questions.reviewNote: Turning off unused water avoids waste.

choices: Could we unplug unused chargers at the end of the day?
Only one kind of family can conserve resources.
questions.correctAnswer: Could we unplug unused chargers at the end of the day?

questions.prompt: Which question should a class avoid asking students to share?
choices: What does your family pay for electricity?
How can a classroom reduce paper waste?
Why should taps be turned off when not in use?
questions.correctAnswer: What does your family pay for electricity?
questions.reviewNote: Bills and private home details should not be required.

questions.prompt: Small repeated habits can help conserve resources over time.
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: Conservation suggestions should be realistic and respectful.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.reviewNote: Good suggestions avoid shame and respect different situations.

lessons.title: Natural Resources and Stewardship
lessons.learningGoal: Students will identify natural resources and explain how stewardship guides responsible use.
successCriteria: I can identify natural resources used in everyday life.
I can explain why resources should be used responsibly.
I can connect stewardship to reducing waste, reusing, repairing, and recycling when appropriate.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise identifying resources and making stewardship-minded choices.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that natural resources support daily life and should be used with gratitude, care, and responsibility.
lessons.christianFocus: Students learn that the world belongs to God and people are called to steward resources wisely, not worship creation or waste it.
lessonContent: A natural resource is something from the earth that people use, such as water, soil, trees, minerals, plants, animals, sunlight, and fuels.
Some resources are renewable if managed wisely, while others are non-renewable or very slow to replace.
Stewardship means caring responsibly for what God has made and provided.
Reducing waste, reusing, repairing, recycling, and choosing durable materials can be stewardship actions.
Good stewardship considers people, the environment, cost, safety, and long-term needs.

studentActivity.title: Resource Stewardship Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise identifying resources and choosing responsible ways to use them.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: resources support daily life
steps.text: People use natural resources every day. Water, trees, soil, minerals, fuels, plants, animals, and sunlight all support human needs in different ways.

steps.title: Renewable and Non-Renewable
steps.prompt: Management matters
steps.text: Some resources can be renewed if managed wisely. Others are limited or take a very long time to replace. Responsible choices help resources serve people now and later.

steps.title: Paper
steps.prompt: Paper usually comes from which natural resource?
steps.correctAnswer: trees
steps.feedback: Correct. Paper is made from wood fibres from trees.
steps.hint: Think about wood pulp.

steps.title: Metal
steps.prompt: A metal spoon is made from materials that began as what kind of resource?
steps.correctAnswer: minerals mined from the earth
steps.feedback: Yes. Metals come from minerals or ores.
steps.hint: Think about mining.

steps.title: Water
steps.prompt: Why is clean water an important resource?
choices: People, plants, animals, and many systems need it.
It is useful only when it becomes electricity.
It can replace every other resource.
steps.correctAnswer: People, plants, animals, and many systems need it.
steps.feedback: Correct. Clean water supports life and many human activities.
steps.hint: Water has many uses.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Natural resources are used in many everyday objects and activities.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Resources support daily life.
steps.hint: Look around a classroom and notice materials.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised identifying natural resources.

steps.title: Stewardship Is Wise Care
steps.prompt: Use resources responsibly
steps.text: Christian stewardship means caring responsibly for what God made and provided. It includes gratitude, wise use, avoiding waste, and caring about people affected by resource choices.

steps.title: Repair
steps.prompt: A backpack zipper breaks, but the bag is otherwise strong. Which choice often shows good stewardship?
choices: repair the zipper if it is reasonable
throw away the bag immediately without checking
buy several replacements just in case
steps.correctAnswer: repair the zipper if it is reasonable
steps.feedback: Correct. Repair can reduce waste.
steps.hint: Think about using resources wisely.

steps.title: Reuse
steps.prompt: Which choice reuses a resource?
choices: using a clean jar to store craft supplies
throwing away a container that could safely be used again
printing the same page several times by mistake
steps.correctAnswer: using a clean jar to store craft supplies
steps.feedback: Yes. Reuse gives an item another helpful purpose.
steps.hint: Reuse means using again.

steps.title: Balanced Stewardship
steps.prompt: Which statement best fits stewardship?
choices: Use resources wisely while considering people, safety, and long-term care.

Use resources as fast as possible before others do.
steps.correctAnswer: Use resources wisely while considering people, safety, and long-term care.
steps.feedback: Correct. Stewardship includes wise, responsible use.
steps.hint: Stewardship is not wastefulness or fear.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Stewardship can include reducing waste, repairing, reusing, and recycling when appropriate.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. These can be stewardship choices.
steps.hint: Think about wise care of resources.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised stewardship-minded resource choices.

questions.reviewNote: Natural resources come from the earth.

fresh rain that hardens in a mould
questions.correctAnswer: minerals or ores mined from the earth
questions.reviewNote: Metals come from mined minerals or ores.

lessons.title: Environmental Effects and Trade-Offs
lessons.learningGoal: Students will compare effects of energy and resource use on society and the environment using evidence and balanced reasoning.
successCriteria: I can describe possible effects of energy and resource use.
I can explain that choices can have benefits and costs.
I can use careful, respectful wording when discussing environmental concerns.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise balanced reasoning about energy use, environmental effects, technology, and mitigation.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that energy and resource decisions affect people and the environment and should be compared honestly.
lessons.christianFocus: Students practise truthful thinking, stewardship, and neighbour-love by considering how resource choices affect people and creation.
lessonContent: Energy and resource use can affect society and the environment.
Benefits may include heat, electricity, transportation, jobs, food production, and useful materials.
Costs may include pollution, habitat damage, waste, higher expenses, or health and safety concerns.
Burning coal, oil, and natural gas can add gases such as carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
Students should discuss environmental concerns with evidence, humility, and hope, not fear or blame.
To mitigate an effect means to reduce its harm.
practiceIdeas: Share the student mission for practice stars.
Use the lesson quiz as the scored check.
Review missed ideas before assigning the next Conservation of Energy and Resources lesson.

studentActivityPlan.description: Practise comparing benefits, costs, and mitigation choices.

quizPlan.title: Environmental Effects and Trade-Offs Quiz
quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.

studentActivity.title: Trade-Off Thinking Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise comparing benefits, costs, and mitigation choices.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: choices have effects
steps.text: Energy and resource use can help people, but it can also create problems. A careful student looks at both benefits and costs before making a judgement.

steps.title: Use Evidence, Not Fear
steps.prompt: Think clearly and respectfully
steps.text: Environmental discussions should use evidence and careful wording. Christian stewardship includes truthfulness, neighbour-love, and hope instead of fear or blame.

steps.title: Benefit
steps.prompt: Which is a benefit of using energy resources?
choices: homes can be heated and tools can operate
steps.correctAnswer: homes can be heated and tools can operate
steps.feedback: Correct. Energy use provides real benefits.
steps.hint: Think about human needs.

steps.title: Cost
steps.prompt: Which is a possible cost of using some energy resources?
steps.correctAnswer: air pollution from burning fuels
steps.feedback: Yes. Some energy use can affect air quality.
steps.hint: Think about environmental effects.

steps.title: Atmosphere
steps.prompt: Burning coal, oil, and natural gas can add which gas to the atmosphere?
steps.correctAnswer: carbon dioxide
steps.feedback: Correct. Carbon dioxide is one gas added by burning these fuels.
steps.hint: Think about gases released during burning.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A fair discussion of energy use should consider both benefits and possible harms.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Balanced reasoning considers both.
steps.hint: Avoid one-sided thinking.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised noticing benefits and costs.

steps.title: Mitigate Means Reduce Harm
steps.prompt: Look for wise actions
steps.text: To mitigate an effect means to reduce its harm. Conservation, cleaner technology, careful planning, repair, reuse, and better habits may help reduce harmful effects.

steps.title: Mitigation
steps.prompt: Which choice best shows mitigation?
choices: using insulation to reduce heating energy waste
using more fuel because conservation takes planning
ignoring pollution if a product is useful
steps.correctAnswer: using insulation to reduce heating energy waste
steps.feedback: Correct. Insulation can reduce energy waste and related impacts.
steps.hint: Mitigation reduces harm.

steps.title: Technology
steps.prompt: Which statement about technology is most balanced?
choices: Technology can solve some problems but should be evaluated for cost, materials, safety, and effects.
Every new technology is automatically better in every way.
steps.correctAnswer: Technology can solve some problems but should be evaluated for cost, materials, safety, and effects.
steps.feedback: Yes. Technology choices need careful evaluation.
steps.hint: Look for benefits and limits.

steps.title: Respectful Reasoning
steps.prompt: Which sentence is best for a science discussion?
choices: This choice may reduce energy use, but we should compare cost, safety, and usefulness.
Only one detail matters, so no evidence is needed.
steps.correctAnswer: This choice may reduce energy use, but we should compare cost, safety, and usefulness.
steps.feedback: Correct. It is careful and respectful.
steps.hint: Good reasoning compares evidence.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Mitigation means reducing harm from a problem or effect.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Mitigation reduces harm.
steps.hint: Think about making a problem smaller.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised balanced trade-off thinking.

questions.correctAnswer: heating homes and powering tools

questions.prompt: Which can be a cost of burning some fuels?
questions.correctAnswer: air pollution
questions.reviewNote: Burning fuels can affect air quality.

questions.prompt: Burning coal, oil, and natural gas can add which gas to the atmosphere?
questions.correctAnswer: carbon dioxide
questions.reviewNote: Carbon dioxide is released when these fuels burn.

choices: Energy choices can have benefits and costs.
questions.correctAnswer: Energy choices can have benefits and costs.
reduce harm

questions.correctAnswer: by comparing usefulness, cost, materials, safety, and effects

lessons.title: Design an Energy-Saving Plan
lessons.learningGoal: Students will design a realistic energy-saving plan using observations, criteria, constraints, and respectful recommendations.
successCriteria: I can identify a conservation problem in a shared space.
I can use criteria and constraints to choose a realistic plan.
I can explain my recommendation with evidence and respectful wording.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise designing a conservation plan for a shared space using evidence and respectful recommendations.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn to apply the design process to an energy-saving plan that is realistic, safe, respectful, and evidence-based.
lessons.christianFocus: Students practise stewardship, humility, and service by proposing practical ways to care for shared spaces and people.
lessonContent: An energy-saving plan should begin with observations, not guesses.
An energy audit is a careful check of how energy is being used in a space.
Criteria describe what a successful plan should do.
Constraints include time, cost, safety, permission, materials, and privacy.
A good recommendation explains the evidence, action, expected benefit, and possible limit.
Plans should be respectful and should not require private family information.
practiceIdeas: Share the student mission for practice stars.
Use the lesson quiz as the scored check.
Review missed ideas before assigning the next Conservation of Energy and Resources lesson.

studentActivityPlan.description: Practise building a realistic conservation plan for a shared space.
studentActivityPlan.reward: 10 practice stars after each completed level

quizPlan.title: Design an Energy-Saving Plan Quiz
quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.
quizPlan.focus: Energy audits, criteria, constraints, evidence, recommendations, respectful plans, and action steps

lessons.assessmentPlan: Use the activity to build confidence and the quiz to check independent understanding.

studentActivity.title: Energy-Saving Plan Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise building a realistic conservation plan for a shared space.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: observe before recommending
steps.text: A good energy-saving plan starts with evidence. Instead of accusing people of wasting energy, a student can observe lights, devices, heating, cooling, paper use, water use, or routines in a shared space.

steps.title: Energy Audit
steps.prompt: A careful check
steps.text: An energy audit is a careful check of energy use. In Grade 5, an audit can be simple: list what is being used, when it is needed, and where waste might happen.

steps.title: Audit Evidence
steps.prompt: Which note is best evidence for a classroom energy audit?
choices: The projector was on during lunch when no one was using it.
The room feels like it probably wastes energy.
The class next door must be worse than ours.
steps.correctAnswer: The projector was on during lunch when no one was using it.
steps.feedback: Correct. It is a specific observation.
steps.hint: Look for evidence, not blame.

steps.title: Privacy
steps.prompt: Which audit focus is safest for a class project?
steps.correctAnswer: shared classroom lights and devices
steps.feedback: Yes. Shared spaces protect privacy.
steps.hint: Avoid private family details.

steps.title: Criteria
steps.prompt: A plan must save energy without interrupting needed lessons. What is this?
steps.correctAnswer: a design criterion
steps.feedback: Correct. Criteria describe what the plan should accomplish.
steps.hint: Criteria tell what success means.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Evidence should come before recommendations in an energy-saving plan.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Good plans use evidence.
steps.hint: Observe first, then recommend.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised gathering evidence for a plan.

steps.title: Criteria and Constraints
steps.prompt: Make it realistic
steps.text: A strong plan considers criteria and constraints. A recommendation should be possible, safe, respectful, and clear enough that others can understand it.

steps.title: Constraint
steps.prompt: A classroom plan cannot move plugs or change wiring. What is this limit?
steps.correctAnswer: a constraint
steps.feedback: Correct. Safety and permission limits are constraints.
steps.hint: Constraints are limits.

steps.title: Recommendation
steps.prompt: Which recommendation is strongest?
choices: Put a reminder near the door so the last person checks unused lights and devices.
Tell students they are careless if a light is left on.
steps.correctAnswer: Put a reminder near the door so the last person checks unused lights and devices.
steps.feedback: Yes. It is specific, realistic, and respectful.
steps.hint: A good plan can be followed.

steps.title: Explain the Plan
steps.prompt: Which explanation best supports a recommendation?
choices: The projector was unused during lunch three times, so turning it off then could reduce wasted electricity.
I like posters, so the plan must work.
The plan is best because no one should ask questions.
steps.correctAnswer: The projector was unused during lunch three times, so turning it off then could reduce wasted electricity.
steps.feedback: Correct. It uses evidence and explains the expected benefit.
steps.hint: Look for observation plus reason.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A good plan can include a possible limit or trade-off.
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Honest plans can name limits.
steps.hint: Real plans are not perfect.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised designing an energy-saving plan.

choices: a careful check of how energy is being used
a guess about who is wasting energy
a rule that bans every device
questions.correctAnswer: a careful check of how energy is being used

choices: The computer cart was left plugged in after all devices were charged.
This room is worse than every other room.
questions.correctAnswer: The computer cart was left plugged in after all devices were charged.

questions.reviewNote: Shared spaces avoid private family details.
